$comment: Per-suite pixel tolerances against the LibreOffice oracle.
`maxDiffRatio` is the fraction of pixels allowed to differ by more than
`threshold` (pixelmatch's 0..1 perceptual distance). Every tolerance has a written
reason. Widening one is a decision to record here, not a knob to turn quietly — if a
diff grows, the first question is whether the viewer regressed, and the second is
whether the oracle is the thing that is wrong.
The oracle is LibreOffice, not PowerPoint. It antialiases differently, hints text
differently, and rasterises effects differently, so a tolerance of zero is not
achievable for anything with text in it. For the milestones where fidelity matters
most (m2, m4), keep PowerPoint-exported references for manual spot checks.

suites.reason: A blank slide is flat white. Anything above noise here is a real bug.
One text box and one rectangle. The rectangle should be near-exact; the tolerance is almost entirely the text's antialiasing and hinting.

Text-heavy by design. LibreOffice's line breaking and glyph rasterisation differ from a browser's even when the wrap points agree, and a single word moving to another line lights up a large fraction of the slide. Watch the trend, not the absolute number; check wrap points via debugTrace when it moves.

Preset geometry is generated by our own path builder rather than transcribed from the ECMA-376 tables, so curves on the more elaborate presets differ by a pixel or two along their edges. Fills and positions should be exact.

The inheritance suite: every shape takes its position, size and formatting from the layout and master. Text dominates the diff, so the tolerance matches m2. A *positional* error would blow well past this, which is exactly what this suite is for.
Table borders land on half-pixel boundaries and LibreOffice snaps them differently, so every rule contributes a line of differing pixels. Cell text carries the rest.

Deliberately loose. Gaussian shadow radii, gradient interpolation and alpha compositing are all approximations that LibreOffice makes differently from a browser; matching it closely would mean matching its bugs. Regressions show as structural changes, not as a drifting ratio.
